candidateRows: Contingent beings and their totality require an external sufficient reason terminating in a being that cannot fail to exist.
This is the principal constructive argument offered to establish God's existence through the contingency of experienced beings and the world.
After identifying contingency as his main line, Copleston moves from dependent beings through their aggregate to an external, self-explanatory necessary being.
Necessity applies significantly only to analytic propositions, so a necessary being is admissible only if denying its existence is self-contradictory.
The objection challenges the intelligibility of the necessary being required by the contingency argument at its central inferential step.
Copleston's inference from contingent beings to a being that cannot fail to exist.
Russell begins his response by restricting necessity to analytic propositions and demanding that nonexistence of the proposed being entail a contradiction.
Given an empirically discovered contingent being, the hypothetical proposition that a necessary being exists follows with necessity.
The move directly repairs the contested modal inference by separating the necessary conditional from the experiential discovery of contingency.
Russell's restriction of necessity to analytic propositions and denial of an intelligible necessary being.
Copleston treats the inference as a necessary conditional while acknowledging that the existence of its contingent premise must be learned through experience.
The notions of necessary and contingent beings lack significance outside a rejected logical framework, because necessity applies to propositions rather than things.
This denies that the modal categories supporting Copleston's entire metaphysical argument can meaningfully characterize existing beings at all.
Copleston's claim that an experienced contingent being entails the existence of a necessary being.
Russell responds that the disputed vocabulary has no usable interpretation for beings and confines meaningful necessity to analytic propositions.
Treating a being's essence as involving existence revives the ontological argument, but existence is not a predicate and no named subject can exist analytically.
The move attacks the proposed necessary being by arguing that existence cannot be contained in an essence or asserted analytically of a named subject.
Copleston's definition of a necessary being as one that must exist and cannot fail to exist.
Russell recasts Copleston's necessary being as an ontological argument and objects that meaningful existence attaches to descriptions, not as a predicate of named subjects.
God's existence is inferred from experience rather than from an a priori grasp of divine essence, after which essence and existence must be identified.
This preserves the contingency argument against the ontological-argument objection while explaining why the inferred terminus cannot require a further reason.
Russell's objection that a necessary being illegitimately makes existence analytic or part of a subject's essence.
Copleston says experience first establishes the being, while the identity of divine essence and existence follows because otherwise a reason beyond God would be required.
Although particular things may have causes, there is no reason to suppose that their totality has any cause whatsoever.
The objection targets the aggregation step that moves from explanations of individual contingent things to an explanation of the world as a whole.
Copleston's demand to extend causal or sufficient-reason inquiry from particular objects to their totality.
Russell accepts ordinary causal inquiry within the world but denies that observation of particular causes supplies any basis for a cause of the whole.
Mystical experience is best explained by an objective transcendent cause because its basic character cannot be explained adequately as purely subjective.
This is the principal constructive case concerning whether religious experience supplies grounds for affirming an objective divine reality.
Copleston disclaims strict proof, describes a loving awareness of a transcendent and nonconceptual object, and argues that an objective cause best explains it.
Private mystical reports do not establish God because equally convinced reports concern demons or Satan, which Copleston would not accept on the same basis.
The parity objection directly contests the evidential force of religious experience by showing that the proposed method supports incompatible supernatural conclusions.
Copleston's claim that mystical experience is best explained by an objectively existing transcendent divine cause.
Russell argues that recorded mystical conviction must be treated like other testimony and cannot favor God when phenomenologically similar experiences support Satan or demons.
A profound and wholesome transformation caused by an experience is not evidence that the experience involved any reality outside the subject.
The move rebuts the proposed use of morally beneficial consequences as corroboration for the objective reference or truth of mystical experience.
Copleston's appeal to the transformed and benevolent lives of mystics as support for their experiential claims.
Russell observes that experiences can deeply improve a person's character without involving anything external and denies that wholesome effects verify an external interpretation.
A morally beneficial response to a loved historical or fictional figure does not establish that the figure actually exists.
The counterexample directly challenges the claimed evidential connection between beneficial religious experience and an independently existing divine object.
Copleston's claim that a beneficial effect supports the mystic's veracity and experience.
After Copleston distinguishes experiential veracity from doctrinal interpretation, Russell invokes beneficial attachment to nonexistent historical or fictional figures.
Identifying love of genuine goodness with love of God risks defining God as goodness rather than independently establishing God's existence.
The challenge exposes a possible definitional substitution or circularity at the center of Copleston's interpretation of value and religious love.
Copleston's claim that love directed toward objective value can count as love directed toward God.
Copleston has argued that even love associated with a fictional person is really directed toward an objectively valid value that excites love.
Goodness is not identical with God, but reflects and proceeds from God, although interpreting conduct this way presupposes God's existence.
The move clarifies the proposed relation between God and objective goodness while acknowledging that this interpretation cannot itself prove God.
Russell's objection that Copleston may simply mean by God the totality or system of whatever is good.
Russell has pressed Copleston to say whether every love of something good is, by definition, a love of God requiring further argument.
Moral distinctions need no external theological justification because they can be recognized through feeling much as colors are distinguished through perception.
This supplies Russell's foundational non-theistic account of moral discrimination, against which Copleston's argument from moral value is directed.
Copleston's demand for a justification and faculty underlying the distinction between moral good and evil.
Russell has denied that things are good because they participate in divine goodness, prompting Copleston to ask how he justifies moral distinctions.
If morality rests only on feeling, no objective criterion remains for distinguishing atrocious conduct from exemplary conduct when sentiments differ.
The objection tests whether Russell's account can condemn extreme wrongdoing objectively rather than merely record disagreement among emotional responses.
Russell's view that moral differences are grounded in feelings analogous to perceptual discrimination.
Russell has allowed that opposed people can experience different emotional appeals and compared moral error with abnormal color perception.
Widespread awareness of moral obligation is best explained by a transcendent ground of value and a non-arbitrary author of moral law.
This is the affirmative side's direct moral argument for God, linking common moral experience to transcendent value and moral authority.
The discussion has moved from subjective feeling and consequences to whether moral obligation has a basis capable of supporting objective moral judgment.
There is no absolute moral law because moral requirements change historically, with practices such as cannibalism once regarded as duties.
Historical variation directly attacks the asserted universality and absoluteness needed for Copleston's inference from moral law to God.
Copleston's claim that moral obligation is explained by a transcendent ground and an absolute moral law.
Copleston has argued that atheists who deny God are logically driven to deny absolute values and an absolute moral law.
Culturally conditioned moral precepts remain criticizable only if an objective ideal order exists, and recognizing that order implies a divine foundation.
The move answers cultural variation while preserving the core inference from moral criticism and obligation to an objective divine ground.
Russell's objection that divergent consciences imply either selective divine speech or divine communication of false precepts.
Russell has argued that radically different moral consciences undermine the proposal that God communicates or grounds moral requirements.
The sense of moral obligation can be explained as imagined disapproval produced by customs, taboos, environment, and education.
This provides the principal naturalistic rival explanation for moral obligation and directly contests the need for a transcendent moral lawgiver.
Copleston's contention that the categorical sense of ought cannot be conveyed or explained through parents and social instruction.
Copleston has conceded that education explains changing precepts but denies that it can explain the irreducible obligatory form of morality.
Contingent existence requires a necessary being, while Russell's moral and logical positions fail to explain obligation or justify refusing existential metaphysics.
The closing synthesis consolidates the affirmative case on contingency, moral experience, and the limits of Russell's analytic approach to existential questions.
Russell's rejection of necessary-being explanation, objective moral grounding, and broader metaphysical claims about existence.
After extended exchanges on consequences, conditioning, and moral objectivity, Copleston summarizes both his metaphysical and moral arguments against Russell's position.
